abstract:
Many computer vision systems require low-cost segmentation algorithms based on deep learning, either because of the enormous size of input images or limited computational budget. Common solutions uniformly downsample the input images to meet memory constraints, assuming all pixels are equally informative. In this work, we demonstrate that this assumption can harm the segmentation performance
because the segmentation difficulty varies spatially (see Figure 1 “Uniform”). We combat this problem by introducing a learnable downsampling module, which can be optimised together with the given segmentation model in an end-to-end fashion. We formulate the problem of training such downsampling module as optimisation of sampling density distributions over the input images given their low-resolution views. To defend against degenerate solutions (e.g. over-sampling trivial regions like the backgrounds), we propose a regularisation term that encourages the sampling locations to concentrate around the object boundaries. We find the downsampling
module learns to sample more densely at difficult locations, thereby improving the segmentation performance (see Figure 1 "Ours"). Our experiments on benchmarks of high-resolution street view, aerial and medical images demonstrate substantial improvements in terms of efficiency-and-accuracy trade-off compared to both uniform downsampling and two recent advanced downsampling techniques.

# LEARNING TO DOWNSAMPLE FOR SEGMENTATION OF ULTRA-HIGH RESOLUTION IMAGES

Anonymous authors

Paper under double-blind review

![](images/871c82aa787db57b2cb3c7f5840cc19a8e201b033af29233a20cac82d9eb8e60.jpg)  
Figure 1: Semantic segmentation with learnt deformed downsampling on cancerous histology image. We propose a method for learning to downsample ultra high-resolution images (top-row) that reflects the importance of each location. The aim is to learn non-uniform downsampling (blue dots on the images) to preserve information that guides segmentation and ignore image content that does not contribute (e.g. dark green arrows) thereby enabling low-cost semantic segmentation on low-resolution downsampled images. This strategy helps identify small regions such as the cancerous regions with abnormal tissues (yellow arrows); see masked ground truth and predictions in middle-row. Compared to baseline standard uniform downsampling (referred to as "Uniform") our method (referred to as "Ours") samples more densely at important semantic regions (yellow arrows) and leads to more accurate segmentation (see bottom-row).

# ABSTRACT

Segmentation of ultra-high resolution images with deep learning is challenging because of their enormous size, often consisting of millions or even billions of pixels. Common solutions drastically downsample the image uniformly to meet memory constraints, implicitly assuming all pixels are equally important. However this assumption is not true and compromises the performance of deep learning techniques that have proved powerful on standard-sized images. For example with uniform downsampling, see the arrow pointed regions in Fig. 1, the unhealthy cells (yellow arrows) do not have enough corresponding samples while the less informative "background" regions (green arrows) are oversampled, and lead to a negative effect on the segmentation prediction from the low-resolution downsampled image. In this work we show that learning the spatially varying downsampling strategy jointly with segmentation offers advantages in segmenting large images with limited computational budget. Fig. 1 shows that our method adapts the sampling density over different locations so that more samples are collected from the small important regions (yellow arrows) and less from the others (green arrows), which in turn leads to better segmentation accuracy. We show on two public and one local high-resolution datasets across different domains that our method consistently learns sampling locations preserving more information and leads to 1) boosted  $3\%$  to  $10\%$  absolute mIoU (up to  $25\%$  in class-wise IoU) and 2) better cost-performance trade-off saving up to  $90\%$  calculations over baseline methods. Code will be available here.

# 1 INTRODUCTION

Many automated processes such as auto-piloting, geospatial analysis and medical image processing rely on good semantic segmentation over ultra-high resolution images with millions or even billions of pixels. Exemplary applications include urban scene analysis with camera array images ( $>25000 \times 14000$  pixels) (Wang et al., 2020), geospatial analysis with satellite images ( $>5000 \times 5000$  pixels) (Maggiori et al., 2017) and histopathological analysis with whole slide images ( $>10,000 \times 10,000$  pixels) (Srinidhi et al., 2019). Challenges arise when applying deep learning (DL) methods on those ultra-high resolution images, like those in Srinidhi et al. (2019); Chen et al. (2019); Marin et al. (2019), due to GPU memory constraints.

To speed up performance and adapt to memory requirements or data transmission latency, it is common to uniformly downsample the whole input images, then train the segmentation network and make predictions at lower resolution (locally or remotely), and finally upsample low-resolution prediction back to the original resolution (as summarised in Fig. 2 (a)). However, the uniform downsampling approach, which we refer to as "uniform", treats all pixels as equally important. This generally leads to reduced performance when directly applying DL approaches, which perform best without downsampling on datasets where images have more manageable size like in Chen et al. (2016); Sun et al. (2019). For example, in segmentation problems that require finding "needles in a haystack" — a certain small positive foreground is more important than the rest large negative background (e.g., like tumours in histology images as in Fig. 1), more samples should be drawn from foreground than background and uniform downsampling may be suboptimal.

Based on a similar intuition, Marin et al. (2019) recently postulated that for better segmentation quality more pixels should be picked near semantic boundaries and thus proposed to separately train an "edge-based" network from ground truth semantic boundaries for content-adaptive sampling, as summarised in Fig. 2 (b), and achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) result. However the sampling density around boundaries depends on fixed hyper-parameters and the effectiveness of using a single "best fit" configuration is highly questionable given the large pattern variation in ultra-high resolution images. Secondly, it is unknown how well the "edge-based" (Marin et al., 2019) approach would perform when label boundaries are less informative. For example, cancerous regions in Fig. 1 or forest regions in satellite images (Demir et al., 2018) are annotated based on higher-level semantic information rather than nuclei or tree edges, respectively.

In this work, we start with a motivational experiment to investigate the barriers of current SOTA. We demonstrate that the segmentation performance of the "edge-based" method (Marin et al., 2019) with a fixed sampling density around edges is sub-optimal, as the optimal sampling density varies spatially according to local patterns in different areas. Secondly, motivated by this finding, we then introduce deformation module, a learnable down sampler, that is trained jointly in an end-to-end fashion with any segmentation model (Fig. 2 (c)) learns to adapt sampling density according to the local image contents. The downsampled image guided by the deformation module results in a deformed low-resolution image and hence the name. The deformation module processes a downsampled version of the given ultra high-resolution image to estimate a sampling density distribution hence lightweight and can be used to augment a wide range of existing segmentation architectures. We demonstrate the general utility of our approach using three datasets: DeepGlobe (Demir et al., 2018) and a local Prostate Cancer Histology dataset ("PCa-Histo") are datasets consisting of ultra high-resolution aerial and whole slide pathological images. We also use the popular Cityscapes dataset (Cordts et al., 2016) since it provides a familiar platform for demonstration and evaluation. In all datasets we show that a lightweight implementation of the deformation module can more flexibly adjust the sampling density according to local content than baseline methods. This can consistently boost the segmentation performance and save computational costs.

![](images/9a9156137d0acae2f63d83e698aac00b16cb11957d8bddaa6dc2da152b07b1f8.jpg)  
Figure 2: Comparing training pipelines of (a) "uniform" (b) "edge-based" (Marin et al., 2019) and (c) our proposed "deformation" approaches. Low resolution prediction are uniform/non-uniform upsampled to original resolution at inference.

# 2 RELATED WORKS

Different sampling strategies have been developed to improve the performance of CNNs. We group these methods into three main categories: feature aggregating and sampling, image sampling as pre-processing for classification, image sampling as pre-processing for segmentation.

# 2.1 FEATURE AGGREGATING AND SAMPLING

One key limitation of traditional CNNs is the fix-sized sampling window (i.e. convolutional kernel) restricted information "visible" to the network. Attempts have been made through either aggregating multiple scaled samplings or shifting sampling locations directly. With the former approach, various multi-scale architectures (Chen et al., 2014; 2016; Hariharan et al., 2015) have shown the importance of sampling multiple-scale information, but the aggregation process is less efficient because inputs/features need to be re-scaled multiple times. Dilated convolution (Yu & Koltun, 2015) shift sampling locations at multiple distances to collect multiscale information therefore avoided inefficient re-scaling. Such shifting is however limited to fixed geometric structures of sampling window, therefore deformable convolutional networks (DCNs) (Dai et al., 2017) propose to learn sampling offsets to augment each sampling location at feature level can improve segmentation performance. Although DCNs share similarities with our approach, they are complementary to ours because we focus on learning a better image downsampling as pre-processing so that 1) maximal information can be kept at minimal computation cost at segmentation and 2) it can be flexibly plug-in to existing segmentation networks.

# 2.2 IMAGE SAMPLING AS PRE-PROCESSING FOR CLASSIFICATION

With the intuition that per-image labelling can be predicted by an improved sampling of the image to reduce computation cost, several learnt image sampling methods have been developed. Spatial Transformer Networks (STN) (Jaderberg et al., 2015) introduce a layer that estimates a parametrized affine, projective and splines transformation from an input image to recover data distortions and thereby improve image classification accuracy. Recasens et al. (2018) proposed to jointly learn a saliency-based network and "zoom-in" to salient regions when downsampling an input image for classification. Similarly, Katharopoulos & Fleuret (2019) uses attention weights to guide sub-sampling an informative subset to reduce the computational burden. However, an end-to-end trained downsampling network has not been proposed so far for per-pixel segmentation. More importantly joint optimising the downsampling network for segmentation is more challenging than the per-image classification, due to potential oversampling at trivial locations, as we will show in this work, and hence we propose an edge-loss inspired by Marin et al. (2019) to regularise the training.

# 2.3 IMAGE SAMPLING AS PRE-PROCESSING FOR SEGMENTATION

On learning the sampling for image segmentation, the patch-based or region-proposal approaches aiming to learn optimal crop at each location to reduce the computational cost and improve accuracy, either separately (Girshick et al., 2014; He et al., 2017) or jointly (Jin et al., 2020). However this approach is less computational efficient at inference because each cropped region needs to be segmented individually. Non-uniform grid representation modifying the entire input images to alleviate the memory cost, such as meshes (Wang et al., 2018; Gkioxari et al., 2019), signed distance functions (Mescheder et al., 2019), and octrees (Tatarchenko et al., 2017). However none of those approaches is optimised specifically for segmentation. The closest work to ours is by Marin et al. (2019), who proposed reducing the computational cost by separately training an "edge-based" downsampling network, prior to segmentation, to encourage denser sampling around object edges, achieving SOTA results. However the "edge-based" approach is constrained by fixed sampling density around edges and is therefore less flexible when label edges are less informative. Here in this work we 1) first demonstrate empirically that the choice of sampling density around edges indeed considerably influences the segmentation performance across different locations and hence the barrier of SOTA; 2) Secondly, motivated by this finding, we then propose and demonstrate a jointly trained downsampling system that can adjust sampling more flexibly and boost the performance robustly, despite the variation of edge informativeness across different datasets.

# 3 METHODS

In this section, we first formulate the basic components associated with this study in section 3.1. We then perform a motivation experiment in section 3.2 to illustrate the impact of fixed sampling density around the edge on segmentation performance and its spatial variation across the image. Motivated by the finding, we propose the deformation module, the jointly trained down sampler for segmentation,

in section 3.3. To ease the joint optimisation challenge of oversampling at the trivial locations, a regularisation term is proposed in section 3.4.

# 3.1 PROBLEM FORMULATION

Sampling method: Let  $\mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}$  be a high-resolution image of an arbitrary size H, W, C. A sampler  $\mathbf{G}$  takes  $\mathbf{I}$  as input and computes a downsampled image  $\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{I})$ , where  $\mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times w \times C}$ . Consider a relative coordinate system such that  $\mathbf{I}[u, v]$  is the pixel value of  $\mathbf{I}$  where  $u, v \in [0,1]$ . And an absolute coordinate system such that  $\mathbf{J}[i, j]$  is the pixel value of  $\mathbf{J}$  at coordinates  $(i, j)$  for  $i \in \{1,2,\dots,h\}, j \in \{1,2,\dots,w\}$ . Essentially, the sampler  $\mathbf{G}$  computes a mapping between  $(i, j)$  and  $(u, v)$ . Practically, sampler  $\mathbf{G}$  contains two functions  $\{\mathbf{g}^0, \mathbf{g}^1\}$ , such that for a downsampled image  $\mathbf{J} = \{\mathbf{J}[i, j]\}$  we have sampling operator<sup>1</sup>:

$$
\mathbf {J} [ i, j ] := \mathbf {I} \left[ \mathbf {g} ^ {0} (i, j), \mathbf {g} ^ {1} (i, j) \right] \tag {1}
$$

Segmentation and non-uniform upsampling: In this work we discuss model agnostic downsampling and upsampling methods, and therefore any existing segmentation model can be applied. Here we denote the segmentation network  $\mathbf{S}_{\phi}$ , parameterised by  $\phi$ , that takes as an input a downsampled image  $\mathbf{J}$  and makes a prediction  $\mathbf{S}_{\phi}(\mathbf{J})$  in the low-resolution space. The upsampling process consists of a reverse sampler  $\mathbf{G}^{-1}()$  reverses the mapping of each pixel at coordinates  $(i,j)$  of the sampled image  $\mathbf{J}$  back to coordinates  $(u,v)$  in the high-resolution domain, and an interpolator  $\operatorname{Int}()$  calculates the missing pixels to get final prediction  $\operatorname{Int}(\mathbf{G}^{-1}(\mathbf{J}))$ . In this work, we use the nearest neighbour as  $\operatorname{Int}()$ .

# 3.2 MOTIVATIONAL STUDY: INVESTIGATING THE BARRIER OF THE SOTA

Disentangle the intrinsic interpolation error: Marin et al. (2019) assume sampling optimised by an "edge-based" objective can reduce segmentation error. While the evaluation (e.g. with IoU) is applied only after interpolation involves a compound of segmentation and interpolation error makes their relationship unclear. We propose to disentangle the intrinsic interpolation error independent of the segmentation error by assuming a perfect segmentation at downsampled space. In specific we calculate IoU( $\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Y}'$ ), where  $\mathbf{Y}' = \mathrm{Int}(\mathbf{G}^{-1}(\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{Y})))$  indicating the same non-uniform downsampling/upsampling process is applied to the label  $\mathbf{Y}$ .

Barrier of the SOTA: The "edge-based" approach (Marin et al., 2019), separately train a non-uniform down-sampler  $\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{e}}$  minimizing two competing energy terms: "sampling distance to semantic boundaries" and "sampling distance to uniform sampling locations", as the first and second term in equation  $2^{2}$ . A temperature term  $\lambda$  is used to balance the two energies, whose value is empirically recommend to 1 by Marin et al. (2019) and decided the sampling density around edge.

$$
\left. \mathbf {E} \left(\mathbf {G} _ {\mathbf {e}} (i, j)\right) \right] = \sum_ {i, j} \| \mathbf {G} _ {\mathbf {e}} (i, j) - \mathbf {b} [ i, j ] \| + \lambda \sum_ {i, j} \| \mathbf {G} _ {\mathbf {e}} (i, j) - \mathbf {G} _ {\mathbf {e}} \left(i ^ {\prime}, j ^ {\prime}\right) \| ^ {2} \tag {2}
$$

The first part of our work performs an empirical analysis to investigate a key question: "How does the empirically tuned temperature term  $\lambda$  affect the segmentation performance?" To simplify the problem we perform binary segmentation from the 19-classes Cityscapes dataset (Cordts et al., 2016). We generate a set of simulated "edge-based" samplers each at different sampling density around edge (i.e.  $\lambda$ ) and directly calculate IoU(Y, Y') to investigate the interpolation error, best performed sampler is shown as each dot on Fig. 3 (a). A set of different segmentation networks can then be trained with each of the above "edge-based" samplers with IoU of final predictions shown in Fig. 3 (b). It is clear that there is no "one-size-fits-all" sampling density configuration that leads to the best performance for all individual classes, neither for intrinsic interpolation error (IoU(Y, Y')) or segmentation error (IoU). Fig. 3 (c) illustrates visually the variation of the segmentation performance. These observations altogether imply that the SOTA "edge-based" sampling scheme with a pre-set sampling density around the edge is sub-optimal, highlighting the potential benefits of a more intelligent strategy that can adaptively configure the most informative non-uniform sampling configuration to describe the local patterns at a given location.

# 3.3 DEFORMATION MODULE: LEARN NON-UNIFORM DOWNSAMPLING FOR SEGMENTATION

Motivated by the above finding, we introduce the deformation module, a data-driven sampling method that learns spatially varying non-uniform downsampling at each spatial location according to its importance to the downstream segmentation task. Fig.4 provides a schematic of the proposed method.

1The "uniform" approach will have sampler  $\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{u}} = \{\mathbf{g}_{\mathbf{u}}^{0}(i,j) = (i - 1) / (h - 1),\mathbf{g}_{\mathbf{u}}^{1}(i,j) = (j - 1) / (w - 1)\} .$  
$^2$ $\mathbf{b}[i,j]$  is the spatial coordinates of a pixel on the semantic boundary closest to  $(u[i,j],v[i,j])$  
3We simulate the impact of  $\lambda$  to sampler as shown by Marin et al. (2019), with more details in Appendix A.4. The reason is our experiments used original non-square inputs instead of the square input reported by Marin et al. (2019).

![](images/0de3f79ff85990d5df1764b7d699a0311444ea7bdaec30f4748f03c92073a563.jpg)  
(a)

![](images/5439f3559428345020b61a935ca5c677bb9ae8ba1d8e426505424afaef6504c9.jpg)  
Figure 3: Quantitative (a-b) and qualitative (c) evidences that the optimal sampling density around edge varies over classes hence implies the variation over locations. (a): IoU  $(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Y}^{\prime})$  with different "edge-based" samplers each at different sampling density around edge and best performed for each class is highlighted. (b): IoU of trained segmentation with above "edge-based" samplers. (c) Visual comparison of ground truth and predictions with various sampling density for two example classes. Sampling locations are masked on original image in red dots. All experiments performed on binary segmentation on 1/10th subset of Cityscapes (Cordts et al., 2016) with downsampled size of  $64\times 128$  given input of  $1024\times 2048$ . Note three classes are under-represented thus not reported here.  
(c)

The deformation module takes a low-resolution version of a high-resolution input image and estimates the deformed sampler (a non-uniform downsampler) that adapts the sampling density at different pixel locations. Then, the segmentation network processes the input downsampled image based on the output of deformation module, and estimates the corresponding segmentation probabilities.

For each high-resolution image  $\mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}$ , we compute its lower resolution version  $\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{lr}} \in \mathbb{R}^{h_d \times w_d \times C}$ . The deformation module,  $D_{\theta}$ , parametrised by  $\theta$ , takes the low-resolution image  $\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{lr}}$  as input and generates a deformation map  $\mathbf{d} = D_{\theta}(\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{lr}})$ , where  $\mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^{h_d \times w_d \times 1}$ , that predicts the sampling density at each pixel location. Next, the deformed sampler  $\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{d}}$  is constructed by taking both  $\mathbf{I}$  and  $\mathbf{d}$  as input and computes the downsampled image  $\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{d}}(\mathbf{I}, \mathbf{d})$ , where  $\mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times w \times C}$ . Following the same downsampled segmentation pipeline defined earlier, the deformed sampled image  $\mathbf{J}$  can be fed into the segmentation network,  $\mathbf{S}_{\phi}(\mathbf{J})$ , parametrised by  $\phi$  to estimate the corresponding segmentation probabilities. We note here at training the segmentation loss is calculated in the low-resolution space without upsampling by getting the downsampled label  $\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{d}}(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{d})$  with the same deformed sampler.

Following earlier definitions in Equation 1, the deformed sampler  $\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{d}}$  essentially computes a mapping between  $(i,j)$  from sampled image  $\mathbf{J}$  and  $(\pmb {u},\pmb {v})$  from original image  $\mathbf{I}$ , such that  $\pmb {u}[i,j] = \mathbf{g}^0 (i,j)$ ,  $\pmb {v}[i,j] = \mathbf{g}^{1}(i,j)$ . As mentioned, we would like to train the deformed sampler  $\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{d}}$  who samples  $\mathbf{I}$  denser at high-importance regions based on the sampling density indicated in the deformation map  $\mathbf{d}$ . Inspired by Recasens et al. (2018) we consider the value at each pixel  $(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})$  in the deformation map  $\mathbf{d}$  as an attractive force  $\mathbf{d}(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})$  that is pulling surrounding pixels. The force acts on an expanded region defined by a distance kernel  $k((i,j),(i^{\prime},j^{\prime}))$  so that:

$$
\mathbf {g} ^ {0} (i, j) = \frac {\sum_ {i ^ {\prime} , j ^ {\prime}} \mathbf {d} \left(i ^ {\prime} , j ^ {\prime}\right) k \left(\left(i , j\right) , \left(i ^ {\prime} , j ^ {\prime}\right)\right) i ^ {\prime}}{\sum_ {i ^ {\prime} , j ^ {\prime}} \mathbf {d} \left(i ^ {\prime} , j ^ {\prime}\right) k \left(\left(i , j\right) , \left(i ^ {\prime} , j ^ {\prime}\right)\right)}, \quad \mathbf {g} ^ {1} (i, j) = \frac {\sum_ {i ^ {\prime} , j ^ {\prime}} \mathbf {d} \left(i ^ {\prime} , j ^ {\prime}\right) k \left(\left(i , j\right) , \left(i ^ {\prime} , j ^ {\prime}\right)\right) j ^ {\prime}}{\sum_ {i ^ {\prime} , j ^ {\prime}} \mathbf {d} \left(i ^ {\prime} , j ^ {\prime}\right) k \left(\left(i , j\right) , \left(i ^ {\prime} , j ^ {\prime}\right)\right)} \tag {3}
$$

This formulation holds certain desirable properties that fit our goal: 1) the learnable deformation module produces a deformation map with varying sampling density at different regions, the need for this was illustrated in the motivational studies in section 3.2; 2) the deformation module can naturally fit CNN architecture and preserve differentiability for it to be jointly trained with downstream segmentation loss.

This way the sampling density at each location is optimised by segmentation performance rather than a one-size-fits-all solution hence break the barriers of the "edge-based" approach (Marin et al., 2019)).

![](images/a4cb4e732982a1dafefaf611d524983e98f6418fa7caaee19238ded55428654e.jpg)  
Figure 4: Architecture schematic. The deformation module produces the deformation map  $\mathbf{d} = D_{\theta}(\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{lr}})$  that predicts sampling importance weights at different pixel locations. The deformed sampler  $\mathbf{G_d}$  samples with different density at each location of the input image  $\mathbf{I}$  according to the deformation map, where sampling locations are shown as red dots masked on the original image. The low-resolution downsampled image  $\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{G_d}(\mathbf{I},\mathbf{d})$  is then fed into the segmentation module which makes a prediction  $\mathbf{S}_{\phi}(\mathbf{J})$  in the low-resolution space. At inference time, the prediction is non-uniformly upsampled to the original space in a deterministic manner.

# 3.4 SINGLE SEGMENTATION LOSS DOES NOT WORK: REGULARISATION TERM IS NEEDED

Our method is similar to Recasens et al. (2018), which however is only explored for image classification tasks. Transferring the method proposed in Recasens et al. (2018) to segmentation not only needs reformulating the problem as described in section 3.1, optimising the joint system at the pixel level is not trivial due to potential oversampling at easy to segment regions like background. Such challenges have been verified in later experiments where the naive adaptation of the method from Recasens et al. (2018) to segmentation (red bars in Fig. 5) fails to improve both baselines on 2/3 datasets. To discourage the network learn trivial solutions, we add a regularisation term in addition to the segmentation loss. Inspired by the "edge-based" method (Marin et al., 2019) we add an additional edge-loss to encourage denser sampling around the edge. Different to the approach of Marin et al. (2019) 1) we directly simulate a target deformation map without separate training to carry its main message that edge information is useful and 2) fit into the joint training system excludes the heavy dependency to a specific parameter  $\lambda$ .

In specific, let  $Y_{lr}$  be the uniformly downsampled segmentation label, the edge loss  $\mathcal{L}_e(I_{lr},Y_{lr};\theta) = MSE(d,d_t)$ , where  $d$  is the predicted deformation map  $d = D_{\theta}(I_{lr})$ , and  $d_t$  is the target deformation map  $d_t = Edge(Gaus(Y_{lr},\delta))^5$ . To this end, we jointly optimise the parameters  $\{\theta ,\phi \}$  of both the deformation module and the segmentation module to minimise the segmentation specific loss function,  $\mathcal{L}_s(\mathbf{J};\theta ,\phi)$ , and the edge-loss,  $\mathcal{L}_e(I_{lr},Y_{lr};\theta)$ . We also add a weight term to make sure both losses have comparable magnitudes.

# 4 EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS

In this section, we evaluate the performance of our deformed downsampling approach on three datasets from different domains as summarised in Table 1, against baselines described in section 4.1. We evaluate the segmentation performance with IoU and verify the quality of the sampler by looking at intrinsic interpolation error with IoU( $\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Y}^{\prime}$ ). We show quantitatively and qualitatively (section 4.2) that our method can learn the spatial variation of optimal sampling density and lead to a better cost-performance trade-off. We further demonstrate how our method generalise the edge-loss differently than similar work (Marin et al., 2019) in section 4.3. The deformation module is defined as a

small CNN architecture comprised of 3 convolution layers. The segmentation network was defined as a deep CNN architecture, with HRNetV2-W48 (Sun et al., 2019) used in all datasets, and PSP-net (Zhao et al., 2017) as a sanity check in the Cityscapes dataset. We employ random initialisation like as in He et al. (2015), the same training scheme (Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2014), the focal loss as segmentation loss and MSE loss for the edge-loss with full details in Appendix A.6) unless otherwise stated.

# 4.1 BASELINES

We compare our method either with single segmentation loss ("Ours-Single loss") or adding edge-loss ("Ours-Joint loss") against two baselines: 1) uniform downsampling of the input to train the segmentation network followed by uniformly upsampling the prediction ("uniform"); 2) the second "edge-based" baseline is an approximation of method from Marin et al. (2019), follow same reason and scheme as declared in motivational section 3.2, which is the best-performed result from a set segmentation networks each trained with a simulated "edge-based" samplers represents with different  $\lambda$ . In addition, for a fair comparison, we also perform experiments at the same experimental conditions with square input and compare reported results from Marin et al. (2019) in section 4.3.

# 4.2 QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS

We plot: 1) mIoU and mIoU  $(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Y}^{\prime})$  in Fig. 5 comparing our method against both baselines on all three datasets; 2) Fig. 6 further investigate IoU at per-class level, aiming to understand the impact of different object sizes reflected by different class frequency; 3) lastly, in Fig. 7, we examine the impact of downsampled size and ask could our method learn a downsampling strategy enable better trade-off between performance and computational cost.

In Fig. 5, looking at mIoU, we see "Ours-Joint loss" consistently performs best with a boost of  $3\%$  to  $10\%$  over the "uniform" baseline. We also observe the improvements after adding the edge loss vary over datasets which supported our argument that our jointly trained method learnt to generalise sampling better at different important regions and leads to better overall segmentation accuracy. On the other hand, mIoU  $(Y, Y')$  does not always agree with mIoU, indicating segmentation error and interpolation error are not tightly bounded therefore separately trained sampler may fail and jointly trained system is necessary.

![](images/498940b32087d2f92752802f5484d7983548f21aeeef4604446ccb1586916149.jpg)

![](images/8c5c5c88f722e03b85859498906e496a23af703b10b0b99effa1052f8ae1eaff.jpg)

![](images/433e75e926a8dcbcba202067727d2a6718c5aeceb0e9510d82d29e75b6cf819a.jpg)  
Figure 5: Quantitative comparison of segmentation performance with our learn to downsample strategy, either with single segmentation loss or adding the regularisation edge loss, versus two baseline downsampling methods, in terms of mIoU and mIoU  $(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Y}^{\prime})$ . Results are from three datasets: (a) Cityscapes (Cordts et al., 2016) (b) DeepGlobe (Demir et al., 2018) and a local prostate cancer histology dataset (PCa-Histo).

Class-wise "Ours-Joint loss" achieved up to  $25\%$  boost in absolute IoU, as in Fig. 6, includes improving all low-frequency classes representing small objects, and significantly improved "edge-based" baseline in high-frequency classes representing large objects, either better or close to the "uniform" baseline. Such results verified our joint trained method generalise "edge-based" sampling better to not only small but large objects.

We introduced the novel edge-loss to regularize the training of the joint system, inspired by Marin et al. (2019). Here we measure boundary precision and ask 1) how does it contribute to overall segmentation accuracy? and 2) how differently do the joint system balance boundary accuracy and overall segmentation accuracy than the separate system (Marin et al., 2019)? We adopt trimap following Kohli et al. (2009); Marin et al. (2019) computing the accuracy within a band of varying width around boundaries in addition to mIoU, for all three datasets in Fig. 10 (b). We found: 1) the "edge-based" baseline consistently obtain the best accuracy closest to the boundary, but this does not consistently transfer to mIoU gain; 2) Our joint learnt downsampling on the other hand automatically identify the most beneficial sampling distance to invest sampling thus lead to the best overall mIoU improvement; 3) The learnt most beneficial sampling distance by our approach also turns out to be data-dependent that can close to the boundary (i.e. Cityscapes) or away (i.e. DeepGlobe and PCa-Histo), while edge approach without this adjustable scheme will fail; 4) it also strengthened one key hypothesis that our method is particularly useful when the labelling region is based on higher-level knowledge, i.e. Deep globe dataset and PCa-Histo dataset when optimal edge failed, which scenario is of the future research interests in the vision community.

# 5 CONCLUSION

We introduce an approach for learning to downsample ultra high-resolution images for segmentation tasks. The main motivation is to adapt the sampling budget to the difficulty of segmented pixels/regions. We empirically illustrate SOTA method (Marin et al., 2019) been limited by sampling location fixed constrained to manual designed edge objective, and hence motivate our end-to-end trained method. We illustrate simple extend the method of (Recasens et al., 2018) to segmentation does not work, and propose to avoid trivial solutions by incorporating an edge-loss to regularize the training. Although our edge-loss, despite a simpler approximation, share the same spirit with Marin et al. (2019) we demonstrate our jointly trained method generalises sampling more robustly especially when label edges are less informative and consistently leads to a better cost-performance trade-off. Our method is light weighted and can be flexibly combined with the existing segmentation method without modifying architecture.
